records.text: What are the hættir (verse-forms) of poetry? Three things. Which? Setning (rule), leyfi (licence), fyrirboðning (prohibition). What is the setning (rule) of the verse-forms? Twofold. Which? Regular and varied. How is the regular rule of the verse-forms? Twofold. Which? Tala (number) and grein (distinction). What is the number in the rule of the verse-forms? Threefold. Which? One number is how many verse-forms have been found in the poetry of the chief skalds. The second number is how many vísuorð (lines) stand in one erindi (stanza) in each verse-form. The third number is how many syllables are set in each line in each verse-form. What is the grein (distinction) in the rule of the verse-forms? Twofold. Which? Málsgrein (distinction of diction) and hljóðgrein (distinction of sound). What is málsgrein? Stafasetning (the placing of the staves, i.e. letters) distinguishes all diction, while hljóðgrein (distinction of sound) is having syllables long or short, hard or soft, and that rule of sound-distinctions is what we call hendingar (internal rhymes), as it is composed here:

the violence of peace-breaking, the king.

the prince has the greater good fortune,
and Gandvík, the sovereign, the land.

records.text: The hendingar (internal rhymes) are to be set in the dróttkvætt (court metre) verse-form in such a way that the latter rhyme in each line, which is called viðrhending (the answering rhyme), must stand in that syllable which has one syllable after it [the penultimate], while the rhyme that is called frumhending (the first rhyme) stands sometimes at the beginning of the line — we then call it oddhending (point rhyme) — and sometimes in the middle of the line — we then call it hluthending (part rhyme). This is the dróttkvætt verse-form. In this verse-form most of what is carefully wrought is composed. This is the origin of all verse-forms, just as the málrúnar (speech-runes) come before the other runes.

records.text: What are kenndir hættir (verse-forms with kennings)? Such as this:

records.text:
There falls about the ruler of the fires
of spear-crash [of swords; the warrior], the limbs of the shoulders [the arms],
Hamðir's garment [a mail-coat], where with rings
the kin-prop of the king [the king's kinsman] covers them.
He hides the wood with the battle-boar [helmet]
of the brain's farmstead [the hair], and the dealer
of gold [the generous man], on the hawk's perch [his arm],
the battle-coalfish [sword], the leader, brandishes.

records.text: Kennings are distinguished in three ways. The first are called kenningar (kennings), the second tvíkennt (doubly determined), the third rekit (extended). It is a kenning to call battle 'fleinbrak' (spear-crash), and it is tvíkennt to call the sword 'fleinbraks fúr' (fire of spear-crash), and it is rekit if it is longer. Rekit:

records.text:
The splendid hater of the sea's fire [of gold; the generous man] defends
the wife of the wolf's foe [Óðinn's wife, Jörð = the land].
Prows are set before the steep
brow of the wife of Mímr's friend [Óðinn's wife, Jörð; i.e. the cliffs].
The mother of the Serpent's harmer [Þórr's mother, Jörð = the land] can
the noble all-ruler hold.
Necklace-foe [generous man], enjoy the mother
of the giantess's enemy [Þórr's mother, Jörð = the land] until old age.

records.text: What are sannkenningar (true descriptions)? Such as this:
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text:
Heavy wounds swell greatly,
the strong edge, for bold men,
sharply cuts trusty shields.
The tall prince lives nobly.
Bright swords each warrior stains
hard; the noble king,
— the splendid shield is furrowed wondrously —
rejoices, bright, in a brave heart.
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: It is a sannkenning (true description) to support the word thus with true matter, as to call the wounds 'stinn' (heavy), because great wounds are heavy. And it is rightly said that they 'þróask' (swell). Another sannkenning is that the wounds swell 'stórum' (greatly). Now that is one line and two sannkenningar. In the second line the edge is called strong, and the men bold. In the third it is thus, that it cuts sharply, the shield is trusty; and in the fourth line, to call the king great, and his life noble; next, to call the sword bright and hard-reddened, and 'each one' of the men of the host, and it would be correct diction even if a man were named. The king is called noble. The shield was excellent and was furrowed wondrously quickly. The king, glad, rejoiced in a valiant heart. Now here sixteen sannkenningar are shown in eight lines, and yet they beautify the verse much more if they are not followed so painstakingly. Sannkenningar have three kinds. One is called sannkenning, the second stuðning (support), the third tvíriðit (doubled). Stuðningar (supports):

records.text:
The furiously hard edge, I hear, destroys
fully valiant men.
The deed-bold warrior's death is caused
by the over-daring king.
To the dark-coated hawk of Hlökk [the raven] he brings
increased mouth-reddening [blood],
glory-boasting I hear the prince is,
the terror-daring wielder of the shield [warrior].
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: Here a stuðning (support) accompanies each sannkenning, as when the edge is called 'óhörð' [furiously hard; read óðhörð?] [?], and the men 'fullhvatir' (fully valiant). It is a sannkenning: a hard edge, and valiant men. It is a stuðning when a second word of affirmation accompanies the sannkenning.

records.text: Where are nýgervingar (extended metaphors)? Such as this:
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text:
The wise prince lets the adders of battle [swords]
glide along the scabbard-path,
swiftly goes the mighty snake of strife [sword] out of the straight
baldric-skin [sheath].
The serpent of the swords' quarrel [of battle; the sword] seeks
to find the brook of blood.
The serpent of the slain [sword] rushes to the warm
battle-river [blood] along the paths of the mind [the breasts].
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: It is nýgervingar (extended metaphor) to call the sword a serpent and to make the kenning correctly, and the scabbard its paths, and the baldric and mounting its skin. This keeps to the nature of the serpent, that it glides out of its skin and to water. Here the nýgerving is so set up that it goes to seek the brook of blood, where it glides along the paths of the mind, that is, the breasts of men. Nýgervingar are then thought well composed if the figure that is taken up holds throughout the whole length of the stanza. But if a sword is called a serpent, and then a fish or a wand, or varied in some other way, people call that nykrat (monstrous), and it is thought to spoil the verse. Now the dróttkvætt verse-form is here with five variations, and yet it is the same verse-form, regular and unaltered, and often some or all of these variations are in one stanza, and that is correct, because kennings increase the stock of words, sannkenningar beautify and fill out the diction, nýgervingar show knowledge and verbal skill.
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: It is a licence of the verse-forms to have syllables slow or quick, so that they are drawn forward or back from the correct count of the rule, and they may be found so slow that there are five syllables in the second and the fourth line, as here:
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text:
With the filling of the helmet the king quiets,
— the bold one — of Vindhlér [Heimdallr's head = the sword], the warriors.
He makes with the thin sword
the great rivers of carrion [blood] rush.
The fierce king lets men
possess blood-stained shields.
The ruler of battle reddens for the hersar [chieftains]
— the strong one — iron-grey shirts [mail-coats].
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: In this stanza all the first rhymes are oddhendingar (rhymes at the beginning of the line), and yet this verse-form is dróttkvætt in form.
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: Now shall be shown syllables so quick and set so near one another that thereby the length of the line is increased:
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text:
Cloven I hear the helmet before the king's
sword's edge; the men do their duty.
Therefore the more, where he shakes the shields,
are the polished swords of the company stained.
The prince will not fail, though he
may see the yellow shields of men.
He dares to draw over the brighter
rims of shields the keen sword.
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: Here there are nine syllables in the first and third line, and seven in the second and the fourth. Here it is shown how many syllables at most may be in a line in the dróttkvætt verse-form, and from this one may know that eight or seven may well be allowed in the first and third line. In this stanza all the first rhymes are hluthendar (rhymes within the line), and it contributes to lengthening the line that as many syllables as possible stand before the rhymes. It is the second licence of the verse-forms to have in the dróttkvætt verse-form one line or two in a stanza with álög (additions), or detthent (falling-rhymed), or dunhent (echo-rhymed), or skjálfhent (tremble-rhymed), or in some such verse-form as does not spoil the kveðandi. The third licence is to have aðalhendingar (full rhymes) in the first or third line. The fourth licence is to shorten syllables so as to make one out of two and to take the vowel out of one of them. That we call bragarmál (poetic diction), as Þórarinn Máhlíðingr composed:

records.text:
It did not befall me, where the slayer
of deadly harm [the warrior] dared to fight. [?]
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: But that distinction is set out at much greater length. It is the fifth licence to change tenses within a half-stanza. The sixth licence is to have in the dróttkvætt verse-form samhendingar (same rhymes) or liðhendingar (joint rhymes). The seventh is to have one word of the sentence in both half-stanzas, and that is thought to spoil it in single stanzas. The eighth is to make use of it, even if it turns out the same as a line, or less, which has been composed before. The ninth is to extend a kenning to the fifth determinant, but it is out of kind (ór ættum) if it is extended further. And although that is found in the works of ancient skalds, we now let it be of no use. The tenth is if a drag (a drawing-on) or a stuðill (prop) accompanies the stanza. The eleventh is that 'er' or 'en' or 'at' may be used more than once in a half-stanza, as Refr composed:

records.text:
Happy is he who, of the waves'
high beasts [ships] the steerer, well
— dear to me is the wolf's danger's [Óðinn's]
wine-making [poetry] — is content with his own.
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: And likewise, even if it be in the latter half-stanza, if a man is named or his name expressed by a kenning in the former half-stanza, even though the name is then no other than 'hann' (he) or 'hinn' (that one) or 'sá' (that) or 'sjá' (this). The twelfth is atriðisklauf (the cleaving of a phrase).

records.text: What is tíðaskipti (change of tense)? Threefold. How? That which was, that which is, that which will be. What rule is it to vary the verse-forms by diction alone? That may be done by giving a name to the verse-forms and so distinguishing the first number of the verse-forms, while keeping the second and the third number of the rule. That is, as was written before, to have eight lines in a stanza, and the third number, to have six syllables in a line and the same arrangement of the rhymes.
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: The verse-forms are varied by various phrasings, and this is one verse-form which is called sextánmælt (sixteen-sentenced):
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text:
Toil grows, fields redden,
the shield is hurled, battle sharpens,
gain is won, the leader takes possession,
the spear-socket heats, the wolf is sated,
the shield shakes, shields are bent,
the ash [spear] trembles, truces are broken,
the sword rings, mail-coats are sundered,
spears crash, arrows are stained.
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: Here there are two complete sentences in each line, but the length of the lines and the syllables and rhymes and arrangement of staves are as in dróttkvætt. Now the dróttkvætt verse-form is varied in another way, and again by diction alone.
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: This verse-form people call áttmælt (eight-sentenced):
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text:
The king defends the land with swords,
spears tear wounds asunder,
the painted shield is cut in battle,
the skull springs loose from the trunk,
hosts fall on the field,
the generous prince wages war,
the edge bites a blemish on the limb,
the hair lies severed by the sword.
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: Here a sentence is completed in each line. This is the third, fjórðungalok (quarter-stanza closes):
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text:
The yew-shaker [bow-shaker; the warrior] knows how, for wolves,
— generous with wealth — to prepare a feast.
The battle-swift lord lets the wolf's kin
be content with provender.
The friend of men gives the wolf
a very great beer of the slain [blood].
The wolf gets to taste from the wound
a blood-drink and to redden its lips.
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: Here a sentence ends in two lines. The verse-form which is now to be written is the fourth of those that are varied, but the fifth in the enumeration of verse-forms.
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: This is called stælt (inlaid):

records.text:
Hákon holds sway over both the men
— to the stern-counselled lord the land God
grants with glory —
and, glad, the title of great king.
Power over the wide land has
— the prince of the wind-roof [the sky; God] the fortune
of the young noble has fully shaped —
the generous-minded chieftain.
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

Hákon holds sway over both the men
and, glad, the title of great king,

records.text: This is the sixth, hjástælt (inlaid alongside):
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text:
Manly virtues win praise
for the guardian of men; the worthy people
all bow to the splendid
giver of wealth. The sea stood over the mountains.
The reddening-wand's [sword's] of shields
tending-Njörðr [the warrior] I was able to visit
— that journey was very fitting —
at home. The earth shot up out of the ocean.
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: This is the seventh, langlokum (with long closes):
