records.text:
Hákon rules with bright
— the friend of warriors has won,
the king defends with the sword the lands,
broad-spreading, a great dominion,
the strengthening-Týr of the strife-game [of battle; the warrior] gets
to steer the realm,
the people rejoice at that —
renown, his own kingdom.
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: Here a sentence begins in the first line and ends in the last, and those two lines form a sentence by themselves.
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: This is the eighth verse-form, tiltekit (taken up):
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text:
Over that [kingdom] which — with the mask of the ground's
tribute-fish [the serpent; a gold crown?] he was also hooded [?] —
the people still remember that — his father
earlier had the ruling of.
The battle-risker [warrior] can over the stony
— the prince is endowed with strength — steer,
greatly he rules, and his heart
urges him on, the seat of princes [Norway].
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: Here the former half-stanza is derived from the stanza that was composed before, and that word of the sentence which is called afleiðing (derivation), which was last in the former stanza, belongs to this half-stanza, and that half-stanza is otherwise not correct in sense.
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: This is the ninth verse-form, drögur (draggings):
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text:
Around the wise prince sets
the war-host — and there sink,
the yew [bow] is drawn, under showers of shot,
a shield-wall — men into the grass.
The weapon-reddener stakes out widely,
the gold-breaker [generous man], on the sea, with spears, [?]
sword-song presses on,
the attack-hard one, the rims of the earth.
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: The word of the sentence which is first in this stanza is last in the former one, and the latter is thus drawn from the former. Therefore it is called drögur (draggings).
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: This is the tenth verse-form, which we call refhvörf (antitheses, 'fox-turns'). In that verse-form one must choose together those expressions which are most unlike in meaning, and yet both words must have the same tense and case, if it is to be done well. But for this verse-form it is difficult to find all the words contrary, and for that reason some words are here stretched for convenience. But it is shown in this stanza that the words can be found if they are carefully sought, and it will appear here that most first attempts are open to improvement. Thus it is composed here:
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text:
The ditch's ember's [gold's] seeker [the man] defends
the smooth gap of the land, by the sea [the Firðir],
the shield-harmer's [weapon's] drives the catcher
of the wave's flame [gold; the man] hot cold [threats].
Quickly weighed, the leader parts
peace-harm [strife]; of the sea's sun [gold]
the impeller [the generous man] stops the plunder-custom,
angry, glad, among the foremost trees [men].
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: Here in the first line it is composed thus: 'síks glóðar'. 'Sík' is water, 'glóð' is fire, and fire and water hate each other. 'Verr sækir': it is unlike, to defend and to attack. The second line is thus: 'slétt, skarð hafi jarðar'. 'Slétt', that is even; 'skarð', that is uneven; and likewise 'hafi jarðar'. The sea is 'haf', the land is 'jörð'. But then it is said in one construction that he goes from the sea to the land. The third line is thus: 'hlífgranda', that is clearly spoken as refhvörf, and likewise 'rekr hendir'. He who 'rekr' (drives) carries away, but he who 'hendir' (catches) stops. So is the fourth: 'heit köld', those are clear words, and likewise 'loga öldu'. 'Logi' is fire, 'alda' is sea. The fifth line is thus: 'fljótt válkat'. 'Fljótt' is that which is quick, 'válkat' that which is slow; and likewise 'skilr fylkir'. He who 'skilr' (separates) scatters, but he who 'fylkir' (marshals) gathers. The sixth line is thus: 'friðlæ'. 'Friðr' is peace, 'læ', that is treachery; and further 'röðuls sævar'. 'Röðull' is the sun, and it stands for fire in all kennings; the sea is again, as before, opposed to fire. The seventh line is thus: 'ránsið'. 'Rán' (plunder), that is bad custom (ósiðr); and likewise 'ræsir stöðvar'. He who 'ræsir' (impels) moves, but he who 'stöðvar' (stops) holds back. The eighth line is thus: 'reiðr glaðr', that is clearly expressed; and likewise 'frömum meiðum'. It is unequal to bring a man advancement (frami) or injuries (meiðslur).
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: Here in this stanza sixteen distinct expressions are shown, and most of them are ofljóst (over-clear, punning) to bring into correct sense, and they are then to be taken up thus: 'Slíks glóð', that is gold. 'Sækir gulls', that is a man. He defends 'skarð jarðar, hafi slétt', that is Firðir, so a district in Norway is called. 'Hlífgrandi', that is a weapon. 'Hendir loga öldu' is a man, and he drives cold threats with the sword, that is to punish bad customs. 'Fljótt válkat' may that be called which is quickly decided; that he separates from strife. A king is called 'fylkir'. The impeller of the sea's sun [gold; the generous man] stops the plunder-custom among the foremost trees [men]. These are called the greatest refhvörf.
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: These are the second refhvörf, and here there are half as many lines that are composed with refhvörf, and they are two in every second line, and are for that reason called the greatest.
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text:
Blood furthers — that battle was fought,
rather, concealment is rent — the witness [the wolf].
The shield — while the men the lands
— hard — trembles — begin to guard.
The spear-socket he has over the host, white,
the gracious prince, inlaid, advanced,
while the king's son — men
the cool sword — does his duty — harms.
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: Here are these refhvörf in the second line: 'heldr' and 'slitnar', and 'dul' and 'vitni'. 'Dul' is concealment, but 'vitni' is proof. And in the fourth line are these: 'skelfr harðr', 'taka varða'. In the sixth line it is thus: 'hollr gramr', 'rekinn framðan'. In the eighth line it is thus: 'svalr brandr'. 'Brandr' is a name for fire. 'Dugir grandar', this is composed ofljóst (punningly). Here are also other expressions which are to be taken into the sense, so as to say: 'blóð fremr vitni' (blood furthers the witness), that is a wolf; and 'dul' or concealment 'slitnar' or is broken, 'at hlökk háðisk', that is a battle. And in the second quarter-stanza it is thus, that the hard shield trembles, but the men begin to guard the realm. And in the third quarter-stanza it is thus, that the gracious prince has the white inlaid spear-socket advanced over the host. He is 'framiðr' (advanced) who is set further forward. In the fourth quarter-stanza it is thus, that the cool sword harms men, but the king's son does his duty.
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: This is the third refhvörf verse-form:
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text:
The sail shakes over the maple — of Hugl —
sharply drive the ships — of currents [the ship],
and the billows, around the prince, roar,
shallow, deep, [around] the hater of waves [the ship].
Nor does the wave do plunder to the sea-reindeer [ships],
the loud-voiced one makes for the ships,
the wave before the thin hull
whole is cloven, peace, strife.
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: Here there is one line in each half-stanza that is composed with refhvörf, and two pairs in each, as here: 'grunn djúp', 'hata unna'. And in the latter half-stanza it is thus: 'heil klofnar', 'frið deilu'. These are nominally the greatest refhvörf, and the least of these.
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: Now begin the lesser refhvörf. Here there is one refhvörf in each line:
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text:
The bow frosts at the stem,
the sea falls, but the fir [ship] glides,
the company shuns delay, hard
forward against the roar of the sea.
The straight wind bends the sails,
the web [sail] drives the warships out to sea,
the weather rushes — the prince's deeds
— the ship longs for the harbour — shine.
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: Here there is one refhvarf in each line, and most are ofljós (punning). These are the second of the lesser:
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text:
The ship of the king's men I heard
— the surf rose over the stern — rush,
and the ropes tighten over the crew. [?]
The stud of Róði [ships] leapt beneath the prince.
The crew gets of the heavy warships
the crowded benches manned at length,
the dealer of battle [warrior] lets the stems,
stiff, pliant, sink into the sea.
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: Here there are refhvörf in every second line. These are the third:
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text:
Himinglæva [a wave] strokes the high
— waves part the backwash — decks.
The ugly sea wishes to break
the fair steed of sea-paths [the ship].
Of the pollack's home [the sea] gets to gleam,
the oar glides, around the gracious prince,
the wave stiffens the pliant keel,
cold, the ember [gold]; the vessel rushes.
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: Here there is one refhvörf in each half-stanza. These are the least refhvörf.
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: There is further that verse-form which we call refhvarfabróðir (brother of refhvörf):
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text:
The hand parts from, with the lord,
the oar-handle; winter follows summer,
and the ships by the sea of Lista,
long, take rest from going.
Ale wearies the company of men,
the hall is quickly filled, the true [ale],
and the bowl, at the gift of the góli's [?]
gold, drifts, empty, the full one.
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: Here in the second line and the fourth are those words which are contrary like refhvörf, yet they do not stand together, and there is one syllable between them, and the two do not both end in the same tense. These verse-forms which have now been written are dróttkvætt in rhymes and length of line. Here there are six syllables in each line and aðalhendingar (full rhymes) in the second and the fourth, but skothendur (half rhymes) in the first and third.
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: How is the dróttkvætt verse-form to be varied by rhymes or by length of line? As it is here, dunhenda (echo-rhymed):
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text:
With the clear tarns of horns [drink] he gladdens,
— the horn hardly gets to dry,
mead punishes men's woe —
the prince, the ships' crews.
To the trees of the war-oar-loop [warriors] he gives nobly,
the bold-minded one, old
— he who holds shields before the shot —
the king, waves of honey [mead].
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: Here the word of the sentence that is last in the first and third line is first in the second and the fourth line.
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: This is tilsagt (with explanation added):
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text:
The current of yeast [ale] the noble gives
— I reckon it as ale — to men.
Silence is felled by the surf of men's
— old beer is that — horns [drink].
The health of speech the generous one can
— mead it is so called — grant.
Of ill-humour comes into the choice of drinks,
— wine I call that — the bane.
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: Now is the orðskviðuháttr (proverb-form):
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text:
Eagerly the leader breaks the ember
of the fen [gold]. The hand turns to habit.
The plunder-punisher gives the Rhine's
amber [gold]. Kin is asked after among princes.
Much the ruler trusts the men's
proof. A gift looks for reward.
Rule has the king over the people
for longer. Each grows by following.
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text:
The ice-cold wave I cut with the oak [ship];
the pale planking was
tried, to the meeting with the mighty
ruler. I am known for such.
The breaker received the title of hersir
— loudly; it is fitting to attest the honour —
of wealth [the generous man; I], from the ornament of earls [Skúli],
splendid. It was not sailed for little.
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: This is álagsháttr (the verse-form with an addition). Here the second and the fourth line begin with a complete word of one syllable, and that word follows on from the preceding line, while the five syllables that then remain are a sentence by themselves. This is the first verse-form to be written of those that are varied from the dróttkvætt verse-form with a full change of verse-form, and from here on shall now be written those variants where the dróttkvætt verse-form is changed and varied by sounds and by change of rhymes or length of line, sometimes with something added, sometimes with something taken away.
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: This is tvískelft (doubly shaken):
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text:
The wand-ring's [shield's] sender [the warrior] granted,
war-bold — and I thank for the gift
the generous king of shield-crash [battle] —
a ship-levy district to me, a fine one.
Next the leader found of the waves
the pale beasts [ships] as a gift for the steerer
of the stem-reindeer [ship; me]. The dealer of battle's
splendid munificence I saw.
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: Here it is in the first and third line that the verse-form changes. Here the sound-fillers [the alliterating staves] stand so near each other that there is one syllable between them. The props make skjálfhendur (tremble-rhymes), and the former is the beginning of the line, while the rhymes stand as far apart as possible. But if the first rhyme is in the syllable that is next to the first, then the skjálfhenda does not fail.
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: This is the detthent (falling-rhymed) verse-form:
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text:
Two I remember with the gracious king
sojourns in the world free of sadness.
I had the lot to sit together
with the gold-payer, generous with wealth.
Eagerly the leader gave treasures,
very costly, to the spear-steerer [warrior; me].
Loyal was to the ruler of hersar,
with his many followers, the hoard-clasper [the generous man; I].
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: Here the verse-form changes in the second and fourth line, and the fourth syllable determines the verse-form.
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: This is draugsháttr (log-form):
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text:
The fir I pray the king's favour
to keep, of green shields [the warrior].
The ash got from that prosperity,
of the plank of Hrungnir's soles [the shield; the warrior].
Enjoy, wielder of the war-field's
wand [sword; warrior], many lands,
you were useful to us, until splendid
old age, feller of foes.
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: Here again it is in the second and fourth line that the verse-form changes, and here the third syllable determines it.
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: Now the second poem begins:
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text:
It befits the stout-hearted driver of the din-steeds of the stem [ships; the sea-warrior]
to be mindful;
for the elm-bow's trembling-seeker [warrior] let us increase
Yggr's booty [poetry], in praise of the prince.
For the earl, the swift breaker of the blue paths of the point [shields],
there shall be no lack
— we stir the waves of Hár's hall-cask [Óðinn's mead; poetry] —
of means to raise up the song.
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: This is called bragarbót (poem's improvement). Here the háttr (verse-form) changes in the first and third vísuorð (line). Here the stuðlar (props, the alliterating staves) stand as far apart as they can, and the hendingar (internal rhymes) so that there is one syllable between them. That distinguishes the verse-forms.
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: This verse-form people call riðhendur (swaying rhymes):
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text:
A sharp storm raged around Skúli
of the swift winds of the spear's cloud [shield; i.e. battle],
the sharp edge became, in the blows,
run with the din-springs of the corpse [blood].
The valiant wearer-out of gold [generous lord] prepared blood
for the raven of the sole-stems [the taloned raven] [?],
Páll had to fall forward under the claw
of the eagle's stubborn offspring [?].
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: Here the verse-form changes in the second and fourth line. There both hendingar (internal rhymes) stand together near the end and both close on one and the same vowel, and it is better that a consonant should follow the second of them.
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: This verse-form is called veggjat (wedged):
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text:
Robbery of life came about, to the sore trial
— the sword swung — of the hosts, brought about in full.
The mighty standard-pole pressed stubbornly forward at the assembly [battle],
the banners advanced.
Stripped away, around the king's brother,
the sharp edge the hope of peace from men,
blue spears got to bite.
The yeomen had to run there.
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: Here there is a change of verse-form in the second and fourth line, and there one syllable is inserted, so that two come after it, and the length of the line is thereby increased.
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: Now comes flagðaháttr (troll-wives' form):
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text:
The strengthener of hosts [ruler] fitted out the ship
with the most fair-shielded men.
The prince's brother cut his course
with the most bright-walled [bright-sailed] vessel.
The king drove the horse of the currents [ship],
most tightly wound with ropes.
The sea had to roar against the gunwale
of the most heavy-hulled ship.
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: Here the verse-form changes in the second and the fourth line. Here both a syllable is added and the expression is carried to the utmost [the superlative], and after that syllable there are three syllables, and it is correct dróttkvætt (court metre) if that syllable is taken out.
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: This verse-form is the old skjálfhenda (trembling-rhymed form):
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text:
The promise-keeping helmet-Týr [warrior] cut, from the west to Vágsbrú,
— the wake's cord was carried far —
the high currents
with the cool rudder;
flight grew, when the grim
wave-land [sea] bore the steeds of the surf [ships] before the land,
— the hulls were cooled — among the great host
of the yeomen.
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: Here it is skjálfhent (trembling-rhymed) with aðalhending (full rhyme) in the third line of each of the two halves, but otherwise as dróttkvætt (court metre). This verse-form was first devised by Veili. At that time he was lying on some outlying skerry, having come from a shipwreck, and they were poorly off for clothes and the weather was cold. Then he composed a poem which is called the trembling-rhymed kviða (lay) or the refrain-less drápa, and it is composed after the saga of Sigurðr.
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: This is called þríhent (triple-rhymed):
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text:
Briskly shook, when it was raised,
the very long banner-staff the war-spoils [?].
The host donned — and the king's deeds
were advanced — the full-strong ring-shirt [mail-coat].
The hand played, to the hosts was proven
the cold sword, the all-ruler, the hero among men.
I learned that the broad edge was made ready
for the prince's battle-array; the assembly [battle] stood firm.
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: Here there are three aðalhendingar (full rhymes) in the second and the fourth line, and they all end alike, and a syllable comes before each one.
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: Now comes inn dýri háttr (the precious verse-form):
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text:
He won — he can deny men
dominion, tribute — the judge of mankind [king],
a worthy host, for the hardener of hosts [warrior],
most firmly bound, he who destroys weakness [?].
Loudly, stubbornly, the kindred of men
the prince showered with red wealth [gold],
that the lord of men was able
to offer the people; it came from the king.
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: Here in the first and third line there are two aðalhendingar (full rhymes) together at the beginning, and the third according to the rule of the verse-form at the end.
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text:
The leader begins swift journeys,
greedy breakers beat upon the warships,
the prince's men begin to keep watch,
they pray for the timber's gliding [the ship's advance] at that.
The lucky planking of the ships sweeps
with fitting rims in a strong fair wind,
the waves shake the sides of Haki's
steeds [ships]. It moves on down beneath the keel.
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: Here there are three hendingar (internal rhymes) in a line, and it is skothent (half-rhymed) in the first and third line, but the third rhyme according to the rule of the verse-form at the end, and a syllable follows each rhyme.
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: This verse-form is called tiltekit (taken up):
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text:
And the great helmets [helmeted chieftains] raised up the battle-glad
hoard-scatterer [generous lord],
the slaughter-hastener [warrior] does meet
the din of the metal-shower [battle],
of battle, when the king of the land
to the bold increaser gave
— the noble terror-sweller [warrior] gets all
honour — the earldom.
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: Here the fifth line changes the verse-form, and in that line it carries on a phrase from the first half-stanza, and that line, with its sound-fillings, follows very much after the new skjálfhenda (trembling-rhymed form).
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: This verse-form is called greppaminni (the poets' reminder):
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text:
Who advances fierce battle?
Who is further from stinginess?
Who makes good fortune greater?
Who knows how to diminish wealth [by giving]?
The duke causes battle.
He is furthest from the coward [?].
He has good fortune the more evidently.
He makes away with the gleam of the hand [gold].
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: This verse-form is varied from the dróttkvætt (court metre) form only in its wording.
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: Now comes the verse-form that we call liðhendur (aid-rhymes):
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text:
The noble-minded prince chooses for men,
the wise, the otter-payment [gold].
Often has, before the thruster of the assembly [battle-leader],
Grani's heavy burden [gold] burst.
The sword's reddener wants that there should ride away
the riding-metal of Gnitaheiðr [Fáfnir's gold] [?].
By the risker of battle is scattered
briskly the treasure of the Niflungar.
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: Those are liðhendur (aid-rhymes), where the same letter stands before the hendingar (internal rhymes), and the liðhendr verse-form is correctly composed when in the second and in the fourth line there is an oddhending (front rhyme, the first rhyme of the line) and a skothending (half rhyme) with those rhymes that are in the preceding line, and then there is one and the same initial letter for all those three rhymes.
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: Now comes the verse-form that we call rétthent (straight-rhymed):
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text:
He showers all-red wealth [gold];
the terror-bold sharpener of Hlökk [valkyrie; i.e. the warrior], for men,
I know where on the hawk's fields [hands]
he casts the ring-drops [gold].
The valiant prince lets fall on the hand
for his thanes the fair rain
— the terror-hastener covers men's
arm — of Mardöll's eyelids [Freyja's tears; gold].
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: Here there are aðalhendingar (full rhymes) in the first and third line, and care has been taken to remove the skothendur (half rhymes).
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: There is further the verse-form that we call the lesser alhenda (all-rhymed form): that is, skothendur (half rhymes) in the first line in both halves, as it says here:
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text:
The swift Baldr of the sword [warrior] furthers men
with the treasure of concord [?].
The battle-risker knows how to share out quickly
Grótti's glad drift [gold, the meal of Fróði's mill].
The wealth-foe [generous man] does, with Fróði's
peace-barley [gold], secure his troop.
The many-meadowed one [land-rich lord] covers, with Fenja's
marketable meal [gold], the forearm's realm [arm] [?].
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: The lesser alhenda is correctly composed when it is kept up for the whole length of the stanza. But if it is inserted into a full alhenda, so that some or all of the rhymes in a line there are skothendur (half rhymes), then that is not correct.
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: Now comes alhent (all-rhymed):
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text:
Glory accrues to the king; to men
the gift proves true, the amber of the hand [gold];
the necklace-flinger [generous lord] accustoms himself to great
manly virtues; he made them plain.
Men bear a great abundance
of the sea's handy fire [gold]; with the wielder
peace is seldom made,
of the cool brands of the field-land of steel [shield; i.e. the warrior].
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: Here there are two pairs of aðalhendingar (full rhymes) in every line. This is held to be the most beautiful and the most exacting, if it is well composed, of those verse-forms that poems are composed in, and it is full alhending (all-rhyme) if there are not found in it 'at', 'ek', 'en' or those small words that go with them, unless they stand in the rhymes; but not all men have guarded against that, and so it is not wrong, as Bishop Klæingr said:
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text:
I bade the company onto Geitir's steed [ship],
the work is done for the journey; often
we draw the horse of cargoes [ship] onto the sea,
the troop floats, and we make use of the gliding.
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: This is the stamhendr (stammering-rhymed) verse-form:
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text:
He lets the twisted fragments break
— the prince — of rings before him.
That diminisher of necklaces [generous man] receives for the necklace
fine words about himself.
The arm does gleam with the gleam
of the surf-land [sea; gold] for the trees of shields [warriors],
where the hand, jointed at the joint [?],
bears the embers of the pollack's path [sea; gold].
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: Here in the first and third line one syllable is spoken twice and that is used for the hendingar (internal rhymes), and we call this stamhent (stammering-rhymed) because the rhyme is stammered out twice over [?], and the rhymes stand in the line as riðhendur (swaying rhymes) do.
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: Now comes the verse-form that is called samhent (same-rhymed):
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text:
The appraiser [lord] gives men
the sea-fire of the wrist's skerries [gold on the arm] [?].
The gold-breaker gladdens with gold
the retinue, with exceedingly heavy [gold].
The launcher [of ships; the lord] furthers men
with the red sea-flame of wealth [gold],
where to the worthy king for the treasure
the crew of the sea-steed [ship] give thanks.
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: Here are those hendingar (internal rhymes) that we call samhendur (same-rhymes), because these are all with the same letters and are in the first and third line, placed as skothendur (half rhymes) are in the dróttkvætt (court metre) form.
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: Now comes iðurmælt (repeatedly-spoken):
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text:
The gold-diminisher gives of gold,
the gold-generous one, straight rods to his troop.
I hear that the ring-generous one
— the ring-damager — thrusts rings away [gives them].
The ring-flinger furthers with rings,
ring-fierce, the sword's logs [warriors].
The gold-breaker works on gold
— gold-perilous — full damage.
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: Here samhending (same-rhyme) is used three times, twice in the first and third line, while in the second and the fourth it is carried on as afhending (carried-over rhyme), as in the dunhent (echoing-rhymed) verse-form.
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: This verse-form is called klifat (harped-upon):
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text:
The easily-known one covers with wealth,
the wealth-Týr [generous lord], the bow's compellers [hands] [?].
There to the wealth-trees [men] is granted
wealth in red gold.
For his paid men he adorns the hawk's
— the pay-generous prince — carriages [hands, arms].
The pay-furtherer accustoms the heath
of the falcon's path [the hand] to pay-gifts.
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: Here the samhendingar (same-rhymes) are kept up through the whole half-stanza and take in as aðalhending (full rhyme) the latter rhyme in the second and the fourth line.
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: Now come those verse-forms that are called stúfar (stumps, docked forms):
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text:
The battle-strengthener takes Hildr [valkyrie; battle]
— the ring breaks as a gift — in betrothal.
Sinks beneath Högni's maiden's [Hildr's]
tent [shield] the ruler of the host.
Heðinn's beloved [Hildr; battle] prepares a bed
for most helmet-damagers [warriors].
The slaughter-increased one receives the sword,
the dowry of the Hjaðningar's lady [Hildr].
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: Here the fourth line is docked and a syllable taken away, whereas in the dróttkvætt (court metre) form it should be set with a hending (rhyme).
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: This is the greater stúfr (stump):
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text:
The fire of Yggr's woman [valkyrie; i.e. the sword] rends
for men the tents of the mind [breasts].
The ember of Hlökk [valkyrie; the sword] springs into the temple
of the mind-field [breast] of men, the dark one.
The mind-wall's [breast's] windows [wounds] sweeps
the corpse's bright din-fire [sword],
the fire of battle [sword] is whetted to level
the jutting turrets of life [heads].
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: Here the second and the fourth line are docked.
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: Now comes the greatest stúfr (stump):
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text:
The host-summoner lets the raven
be fully sated of its hunger, the young [lord].
Tread with its soles the eagle gets
the most lifeless skull.
And the grey wolf climbs
the will's stronghold [breast] of the battle-wounded.
Often the she-wolf gets to swallow
— the good prince wills it so — blood.
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: Here all the lines are docked. These verse-forms that have now been written are distinguished into three kinds, because men have composed before in such a way that in one stanza one half was docked and the other half double-docked, and those are háttaföll (metrical faults). The third is the one that is all-docked, because here all the lines are docked.
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: Now comes the skothendr (half-rhymed) verse-form:
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text:
The Skjöldung's descendant sows with showers
of the pennant [spear-showers; battle]; shafts are lifted,
the ground's gust [?] thrusts the war-banners
over the valiant lord.
Banners rage before the prince,
the pole wades into the clash of Gungnir [Óðinn's spear; battle],
strong are the meetings of metal [battles] beneath the standards
around the noble king.
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: Here there are skothendur (half rhymes) in all the lines, but otherwise as the dróttkvætt (court metre) form.
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: Now comes the verse-form that we call liðhendur (aid-rhymes):
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text:
The steersman is wont to magnify
great deeds, of the spears' din [battle],
he knows how to hold, by battle,
the battle-Týr [warrior], land under himself.
The lord tears in every
onslaught Hjarrandi's garments [mail-coats].
Fall there to the filling
of the mountain-wolf the fir-trees of battle [warriors].
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: In this verse-form there are liðhendur (aid-rhymes) in two ways, and the others in this manner: with the former hending (rhyme) in the first and third line.
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: Now shall be written those verse-forms that the ancient poets have composed in and which are now set down together, although they composed some of it with háttaföll (metrical faults), and these verse-forms are called dróttkvætt (court metre) in the ancient poems, but some are found in lausavísur (free-standing stanzas), as King Ragnarr loðbrók composed in this verse-form:
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text:
Shoots at Skögul's weather [battle],
— and the shields do not hold —
Hildr's crashing drift [weapon-storm]
over the white rim of the shield.
And in the sword's sweat [blood]
at the host's sword-drawing
the friend of men reddens the points
— that is the earl's might — swiftly.
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: Here in the first and third line there is háttlausa (form-less, i.e. without rhyme), but in the second and fourth aðalhendingar (full rhymes), and the höfuðstafr (chief stave), which governs the alliteration in the second and the fourth line, stands so that one or two syllables are set before it, but otherwise as dróttkvætt (court metre).
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: Now shall be written Torf-Einarr's verse-form:
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text:
Who could see, than the terrifier of princes,
the very wise, a better earl,
or one more eager to increase
the hard-swelling clash of shields [battle]?
Stands about the Gautr [Óðinn] of the steel-shower [warrior]
no small tumult,
when the people's rampart [defender] the lands
goes to guard against the victory-Njörðs [warriors].
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: Here in the first and third line there is háttlausa (no rhyme), but in the second and fourth it is skothent (half-rhymed) and riðhent (swaying-rhymed).
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: Now comes Egill's verse-form:
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text:
Who would feed with blood the bristling
she-wolf, with the wound's red draughts,
unless the king thus sates
the wolf's greed many a day?
The leader gives wounds
newly bitten by the edge to the wolf.
The host sees the fore-claw of Fenrir's
paw, shaggy, redden.
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: Here in the first and third line there is háttlausa (no rhyme), but in the second and the fourth aðalhendingar (full rhymes) and riðhent (swaying-rhymed).
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: Now comes Fleinn's verse-form:
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text:
The king the helmets' showers [battle]
hardens with reddened sword,
white ash-spears fly,
the mail-coat's plates clatter down.
Hlökk's [valkyrie's] fires [swords] wrench
hard the land of the scalp [head].
The embers of strife [swords] strengthen
the shields' harm around the earl.
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: Here the hendingar (internal rhymes) go as in the dróttkvætt (court metre) form, but the rhymes are set together at the beginning of the line.
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: Now comes Bragi's verse-form:
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text:
There is, of the fire of helmets [sword],
strife expected for the hosts,
there where the earl, for terror,
baits with drawn sword.
One can see the fence before the ground
of the rims of Þundr's [Óðinn's] gate [shields; the shield-wall],
when the friend of men the shield's
chant [battle] was bound to perform.
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: Here in the first and third line the last word is used for the hending (rhyme), but the former word, which should make the skothending (half rhyme), is lacking. And with this rhyme-word there are rhymes in the second and the fourth line, and the one rhyme is a skothending and a liðhending (aid-rhyme), while the other is an aðalhending (full rhyme) with the first. And these rhymes that stand in the second and fourth line stand as in Fleinn's verse-form. It is widespread in the works of the ancient poets that in a single stanza there are various verse-forms or háttaföll (metrical faults), and one may not compose after that model, though it is not thought to spoil the ancient poems.
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: Now come those verse-forms, distinguished into three kinds, that are called kimblabönd (bundle-bonds). This is one:
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text:
The helmet-damager shakes, in Hrist's [valkyrie's]
storm-age [battle], Sigarr's walls [shields].
The king lets break in the wind [of battle]
the sword's bowing boards [shields] of the shields' shores [?].
The steerer of steel-ravens [ships] lets
the storm-wind of strife rush about him.
He receives in Göndul's [valkyrie's] gale [battle]
victory, the leader of the companies of men.
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: Here in the fourth line of each half an aðalhending (full rhyme) is added with two syllables after the line, but otherwise as dróttkvætt (court metre).
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: Now comes the greater kimblaband (bundle-bond):
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text:
The ice of the bow-woman [valkyrie; i.e. swords] is washed
most years by the mighty wave of wounds [blood].
The wise prince lets the helmet-ice [sword] ring
briskly on the waves of the slain [blood].
The strife-glaciers [swords] does the flinger
of necklaces [generous lord], stiff, accustom to the sea of wounds [blood].
The swift ruler lets the host fill
the sounds of the wounds [blood-channels] of the sword's trees [warriors].
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: Here there are two kimblabönd (bundle-bonds) in each half.
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: These are the greatest kimblabönd (bundle-bonds):
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text:
The corpse-gleam's [sword's] rime falls; the season
grows high around the king of wound-oars [weapons],
Mist's [valkyrie's] frost [sword] takes, around Hrist's [valkyrie's] maple [warrior],
the host-cold rim of the shield of men.
The gold-sender breaks, of Hrund's [valkyrie's]
war-wall's [shield's] ground's staves [warriors], the limbs in the storm [of battle].
I learn that by the ice of the battle-field [sword] the old age
— so it falls out — of men is cut short [?].
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: Here a kimblaband (bundle-bond) goes with every line.
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: Now shall be written the hrynjandi (flowing) verse-forms. This is the first:
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text:
The king turns upon the messenger of terror [enemy warrior],
— the wound-gosling [raven] knows that — the hail of attack,
the prince hastens to the storm of shields [battle],
the sword cheats away life in the mail-coat's shower [battle].
The prince holds over the helmet's lands [heads]
the host; so he deals out the bows' drifts [arrows],
showers strike around the valiant king
— we hear of his tumult — of Mist's [valkyrie's] rain [battle].
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: Here the first and third line are augmented at the front with two syllables to establish the verse-form, but if these are taken away, then what is left is like dróttkvætt (court metre), and from the second and fourth line one may take out the word that two syllables belong to, the fifth and the sixth in the line, and then that line too is dróttkvætt. In the hrynhent (flowing-rhymed) verse-forms there are most often eight syllables in a line, but the hendingar (internal rhymes) and the stafaskipti (arrangement of the alliterating staves) go as in the dróttkvætt form. This we call dróttkvætt hrynjandi (flowing court metre).
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: Now more arrangements of the verse-forms shall be shown. This hrynjandi (flowing form) is called trollsháttr (troll's form):
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text:
To the flinging-trees of steel [warriors] taught
the wielder of strife red hoods [bloodied heads],
men steered straight to land
the reddened prow, east of the fjord.
With points pierced the courage-strands [breasts]
of the host of men the diminisher of rings [generous lord].
The king enlarged with sharp sword
the mighty wounds of the brain's ground [head].
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: Here there are eight syllables in every line. Here there are hluthendur (part-rhymes) in all the lines, and three syllables go with each hending (rhyme), and skothendur (half rhymes) and aðalhendingar (full rhymes) and the stafaskipti (arrangement of the staves) go as in hrynhenda (the flowing-rhymed form).
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: This is one hrynhent (flowing-rhymed) verse-form:
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text:
Hesitated little, when he met men,
the battle-tender, to press forward.
The diminisher went, in Hlökk's [valkyrie's] showers [battle],
of Skögul's shirt [mail-coat], before reddened banners.
The land was cleared, and the ruler of the Þrændir
dealt the Ribbungar a heavy death.
Gunnarr thrust beneath the wolf's foot's
grim-set sole the brain's crag [head].
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: This is hrynhenda (the flowing-rhymed form) unvaried.
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: This is draughent (log-rhymed):
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text:
The storm of weapons managed to topple,
merciless, the doomed skull.
The king let meet with blows
the shoulders' crag [head], deserving of death.
The leader ran the mighty ski of the land of spears [shield; i.e. the sword]
along the helmet's slope [head],
the powerful sword destroyed men,
the prince's own, drifted over with flesh [?].
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: In this verse-form there are most often seven syllables in each line, but the hendingar (internal rhymes) and the stafaskipti (arrangement of the staves) are as in the dróttkvætt (court metre) form, and if one syllable is taken out here of the first or third line, the one that stands next after the first, then all the sounds fall as in the dróttkvætt form. So one may also take away in the second and the fourth line the same syllable, and then it is dróttkvætt, though some of it does not become smooth.
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: This verse-form we call munnvörp (mouth-castings, improvisations):
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text:
Destroyed the marauders
the noble duke with spears.
Steel sang over the ruler's
— the she-wolf stood among the slain — foes.
Many a man he made, by a head,
the hoard-fierce prince, shorter.
Thus he knows how to punish robbery,
the wrathful leader, among peoples.
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: Here there is háttlausa (no rhyme) in the first and third line, but in the second and the fourth skothendur (half rhymes).
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: Now comes the verse-form that is called háttlausa (form-less):
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text:
I composed, for men to remember,
about those whom I knew to be foremost of all,
about the valiant princes,
in sixty verse-forms.
Least of all have, honour or gold,
those who caused me to be honoured,
cast onto the ancient sea [wasted them],
— that is glory for me — the princes.
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: In this verse-form there are no hendingar (internal rhymes), but the stafaskipti (arrangement of the staves) is as in the dróttkvætt (court metre) form.
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: Now sixty verse-forms have been set together in two poems, and in addition those eight distinctions which were first arranged in the dróttkvætt (court metre) form with the figures of speech that go with the verse-form, and all these verse-forms are well suited to compose poems after, if one wishes.
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: Now the third poem shall begin, which is composed in the smaller hættir (verse-forms), and yet many of these verse-forms have been used before in praise-poems.
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: Here begins tögdrápulag (the metre of the tøgdrápa, 'journey-poem'):
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text:
Foremost was Skúli —
praise shall not be delayed.
I fashion for the generous king
a many-stranded encomium.
Further shall I bring forth praise
before the increaser of battle [warrior],
— I was dear to the lord —
before the multitude of the host.
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: Here in the second and fourth vísuorð (line) there are four syllables and two aðalhendingar (full rhymes), and the höfuðstafr (chief stave) is placed as in dróttkvætt (court metre); but in the first and third line there are likewise four regular syllables and a fifth, an afkleyfissamstafa (extra-metrical syllable), that is: 'ek' or 'af' or 'en' or 'er' or the like. There there are also skothendingar (half rhymes) and one hljóðfylling (supporting stave) with the chief stave.
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: This is the second töglag (tøg-metre):
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text:
I composed poems, known
to the people, for the king's brother,
three of them; I know that prince
to be surrounded by many men.
Forth shall the fourth [poem] advance
with praises of the battle-glad
breaker of the peace of the bright fire
of the sea [gold; i.e. the generous man].
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: Here the second and fourth vísuorð (line) go as in the previous verse-form, but the first and third line are here without hendingar (internal rhymes), and there are two hljóðfyllendr (supporting staves) with the höfuðstafr (chief stave), as in dróttkvætt (court metre).
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: This is the third verse-form, which we call hagmælt ('skilfully spoken'):
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text:
Many a verse-form of mine
is about the worthy one, [?]
not composed before,
the wise one of the spear-crash [battle].
The clear-minded poet must tell
of the prince's unstinted
splendid expeditions,
the young one of the Skjöldungs [kings].
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: In this verse-form there are skothendingar (half rhymes) in the first and third vísuorð (line), and stafaskipti (arrangement of the staves) as in the dróttkvætt (court metre) form, but in other respects as in tögmælt (tøg-speech). In all töglag (tøg-metre) it is not wrong even if there are five syllables in a line, when some of them are short and quick. It is the way of tögdrápuháttr (the tøgdrápa form) that there shall be a stef (refrain) for the first line, and that statement is to be concluded in the last line of the poem; and it is correct to set the poem with as many stefjamél (refrain-sections) as one wishes, and it is most usual to have them all of equal length, but each refrain-section shall have a refrain as its beginning and end.
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: Now comes the grænlenzki háttr (the Greenlandic verse-form):
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text:
The cutter of the gold
of the seas [generous man] knows how
to make Haki's sinking-steed [ship] gallop
along the terrible track [the sea],
he who from the launching-roller
lets the horses of the moorings [ships],
the praised prince,
go a long way.
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: Here the first and third vísuorð (line) are as in hagmælt, but the second and fourth with aðalhendingar (full rhymes), and two syllables are full-rhymed, and both end in the same letter.
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: Now comes the skammi háttr (the short verse-form):
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text:
Gold does, poets,
gleam; they row;
the men are fit
for hardship, bold.
The oak [ship] may beneath the prince
be content to speed;
then the ruler enjoys
the timber's [ship's] gliding.
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: Here the first and third vísuorð (line) are without hendingar (internal rhymes), but the second and fourth as in the grænlenzki háttr (Greenlandic form), and the phrasing is shorter.
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: Now comes the nýi háttr (the new verse-form):
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text:
The ruler adorns
the dark reindeer of Rökkvi's
lands [ships] with white
shields.
The flinger adorns
the scraped prows,
the flinger of rings [generous man], with the black [?]
stags [figureheads] of the stays. [?]
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: In this verse-form there are four syllables in each vísuorð (line), and two aðalhendingar (full rhymes), and both end in the same letter, and there are no afkleyfisorð (extra-metrical words).
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: This is stúfhent ('stump-rhymed'):
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text:
The sea-current shakes
the roller-steed [ship] of the king,
the plank-ground [sea] bends
the surf-beast's [ship's] rudder.
The battle-hard prince knows
that the dark fair-wind-skis [ships]
break with their prows
the heavy ocean.
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: In this verse-form there are four syllables in a vísuorð (line), but the hendingar (internal rhymes) and the stafaskipti (arrangement of the staves) are as in the dróttkvætt (court metre) form, except that all the rhymes are náhendar (close-set, in adjacent syllables).
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: This is náhent ('close-rhymed'):
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text:
He lets the warships thrust
the sinking-ground of the sea-bench [the sea],
the swift spear-fir [warrior], when
the [waves'] measures fall against the prows. [?]
The war-fierce one sees the retainers
grip the oar-handles,
and the truly good oars
of the strife-elf [warrior] tremble.
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: In this verse-form there are four syllables in a vísuorð (line), and it is not wrong in the first and third even if there are five. There there are skothendur (half rhymes). In the second and fourth there are aðalhendingar (full rhymes), and both together [in adjacent syllables], and the first one stýfð (clipped), but the stafaskipti (arrangement of the staves) as in dróttkvætt (court metre).
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: This is hnugghent ('curtailed-rhymed'):
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text:
Waves stroke the laden gunwales,
the sea-foam drifts in heaps,
the cold bow gets to fling
the salt keel-path [sea] aside.
Over the swans' fells [the sea] with black
[ships] the eloquent ruler drives
forward along Haki's way [the sea]
the storm-beaten skis of the rollers [ships].
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: Here in the first and third vísuorð (line) there are seven syllables and no hendingar (internal rhymes), but it is correct as to the staves. But the second and fourth have four syllables, correct as to the staves, and skothending (half rhyme), and oddhent (with the rhyme at the beginning of the line), and the first rhyme is stýfð (clipped).
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: Now comes hálfhneppt ('half-curtailed'):
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text:
He lets the warships speed in the dawn-red
over the fetter of Mön [the sea around the Isle of Man],
early the young earl,
the all-ruler, sees the breakers fall.
Often the mast is raised above the crew
on the keel's draught-beast [ship];
the gale gets to spread the sail-cloth.
Halyards meet the grasping hands.
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: In this verse-form there are six syllables in a vísuorð (line), but it is not wrong if there turn out to be five or seven. In the first and third line there are skothendur (half rhymes), and aðalhendingar (full rhymes) in the second and fourth, in both places; the first rhyme is regular as in dróttkvætt (court metre), but the second is stýfð (clipped) or hneppt (curtailed), which is all one.
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: This verse-form is alhnepptr ('wholly curtailed'):
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text:
It cuts the wave, swiftly goes
the cold hull, the all-ruler,
the branch-hound [wind] breaks the surf, the sea is shot
by the curved gunwale [ship's side].
Soon it shakes — the breeze drives —
the blue wall [sail], the yard-beard [sail].
The all-worthy earl lets
the masthead-sail stay unfurled. [?]
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: In this verse-form there are four syllables in a vísuorð (line) and two aðalhendingar (full rhymes), and both end in the same letter, and all the rhymes are hnepptar (curtailed).
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: This is Haðarlag (Höðr's metre):
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text:
The praised ruler locks
the outer coasts of the lands,
the kindly one, with blue skis [ships]
and the shield-wall of the prows.
The vigorous earl can [lock] with the points [?]
of the thorns of socket-spikes [spears]
the earth, with the storm-twisted
edge of corpse-adders [swords].
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: In this verse-form there are five syllables in a vísuorð (line), but hendingar (internal rhymes) and stafaskipti (arrangement of the staves) as in the dróttkvætt (court metre) form.
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: Now come those verse-forms which are called runhendur (end-rhymed). They are of one kind. Every runhent (end-rhymed) verse-form shall be with two aðalhendingar (full rhymes), and each rhyme in its own vísuorð (line).
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: This is the regular runhenda (end-rhyme):
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text:
Praise is delivered in four [poems] [?]
before the battle-messengers [warriors],
nor do we spare the tidings
we have heard about the swift king.
I have his journeys,
prepared for praise,
raised up, unlooked for,
before the bearers of wealth [men].
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: This verse-form is maintained with one hending (rhyme) in each vísuorð (line), and such is the runhending (end-rhyme) that separates the rhymes and divides the lines. Therefore this is called runhent (end-rhymed).
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: This is the lesser runhenda (end-rhyme):
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text:
I delivered lore
about the increaser of renown,
the tongue gave aid
with the oar of speech.
The refrain shall magnify
the ruler of the Mærir,
it is fitting to stir up praise
and bring it to him.
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: Here one rhyme runs through half the stanza, and another through the second half. This verse-form is stýðr (clipped) or hnepptr (curtailed) from the previous one.
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: This is the smallest runhenda (end-rhyme):
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text:
Such it is:
the prince has,
and the people grant him,
that renown;
of earls east
of the sea,
the most eminent of men
is Skúli, the most splendid.
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: In this verse-form there are three syllables in a vísuorð (line), and two lines share a rhyme, with stafaskipti (arrangement of the staves) as in dróttkvætt (court metre). And it is found to be so, that it is not wrong if the hljóðstafr (alliterating stave) which governs the kveðandi (metrical form) stands once in front of the main word of the sentence. [?]
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: These are again runhendir (end-rhymed forms):
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text:
Over all the terror [?] of the serpent's
ring-fields' [gold's] destroyer [generous man]
the roller-horses loom above the high stalls,
the steeds of the swan-fells [the sea; i.e. ships].
There is gladness in the serpent's bane [winter] [?]
with the friend of men,
the earl promotes a valiant troop.
Such a one may be called a champion.
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: This verse-form is composed with full runhending (end-rhyme), and there are there most often five syllables in a vísuorð (line), or six if they are quick.
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: This is another:
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text:
The king got a good name,
he is accustomed to battle.
Very excellent is
the magnificent ruler.
He who judges matters
will least find a prince
who so provides for
his men every winter.
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: This is hnepptr (curtailed) from the previous runhenda (end-rhyme):
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text:
I wish to increase the praise,
— of Mist's leeks [swords]
with the sword of the gums [tongue] —
of the diminisher of their ground [shield; i.e. the warrior].
Glory shall be told,
the company may keep silence,
of battle may keep silence, [?]
of the embers of battle [weapons]
the flinging-Móði [warrior].
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: In this same verse-form there are four syllables in each vísuorð (line), but the höfuðstafr (chief stave) as in the dróttkvætt (court metre) form, and one hljóðfyllandi (supporting stave) goes with them.
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: This is the third runhent (end-rhymed) verse-form:
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text:
I know that the hastener of the sword [warrior]
invites [men] into the hall;
good is the house at Hlaðir,
the retinue is sated with ale.
The king drinks merrily,
and as gifts go forth
the beacons of the hawk-perches [gold on the hand]
of the harmer of the wand-ring [shield; i.e. the warrior].
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: This is regular runhending (end-rhyme), and this verse-form is taken from töglag (tøg-metre). Here there are four syllables in a vísuorð (line), or five if they are quick. This is the lesser runhenda (end-rhyme):
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text:
The chain of the hand [gold ring] flies about
where the prince drinks.
Very pleasing to men is
the bench of the kindly bowl.
Among the prince's host plays
the pure-gilded cup,
I say all as it is,
against the skerry of words [the teeth].
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: This is hnepptr (curtailed) from the previous one.
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: This is the smallest:
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text:
And when to the hall the retinue
the leader of the host summons,
often the earl begins to welcome
countless numbers of men,
the gift is ready for paying out
at the gold-breaker's [generous man's] feast.
The people's company sits close-packed
where the greatest distinction is within.
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: This runhenda (end-rhyme) is taken from the dróttkvætt (court metre) form, and here there are as many syllables, and likewise the stafaskipti (arrangement of the staves), as in dróttkvætt.
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: Now begins the fourth bjálkr (section) of runhendingar (end-rhymed forms):
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text:
The retinue makes the prince merry,
the hall is packed tight to the door,
the prince gives wealth without stint,
that is heard far and wide.
Such I reckon the prince's way,
his munificence exceeds his means,
the earl breaks up into small pieces
the twisted gold, strand by strand.
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: This verse-form is hnepptr (curtailed) from the previous one and regularly runhendr (end-rhymed).
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: Now comes the lesser runhenda (end-rhyme):
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text:
Many people go to the prince's halls,
honour is there for all who sojourn,
the king gives out cool gold,
it is best to speak the truth about him.
We hear flat rings being broken,
the friend of men knows how to hate gold [give it away],
I know that the guardian of the land got a nobler [?]
generous spirit than princes of rings.
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: This runhenda (end-rhyme) is taken from the hrynhent (flowing) verse-form.
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text:
Gladly, along with gold, receives
the company of men mead from the ruler.
He lets his troop drink at his home
the fair wine poured in silver.
The golden bowl meets the grasping hands,
he sends men the fire of the Rhine [gold],
no nobler man does he meet,
the best of earls, than that king.
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: This is hnepptr (curtailed) from the previous runhenda (end-rhyme).
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: Here begins the fifth runhent (end-rhymed) bálkr (section):
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text:
The king's expeditions have been told of,
I have made a swift encomium,
the prince will expect that,
that I little spared.
No braver finds
than the feeder of battle-starlings [ravens; i.e. the warrior]
a man, nor more generous,
the marker of blood-gulls [warrior]. [?]
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: This too is full runhenda (end-rhyme).
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: This is the lesser runhenda (end-rhyme), and taken from the hálfhnefst (half-curtailed) verse-form or the náhent (close-rhymed):
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text:
The prince keeps his good fortune fresh,
the greatest achievement follows him,
the ruler gives very well most of
the sea-fire [gold], and unflawed.
The hulls broke the ugly sea,
I sought out the prince at his home,
the whole company praises the Yngvi [king],
I saw the earl's abundance of distinction.
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: This is stýðr (clipped) or hnepptr (curtailed) from the previous verse-form:
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text:
. . . . . . . . the king, [?]
the eminent Kraki sowed gold,
we have heard that Haki waged battle,
. . . . . . . . age. [?]
Sigurðr gave the serpent its wound,
all that was in years gone by,
Ragnarr was thought the most eminent of men,
Earl Skúli is by far the most splendid.
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: Málaháttr (speech-metre):
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text:
I remember from the generous prince,
when to the ruler of the Mærir
I delivered four poems,
fifteen great gifts.
Where may anyone know of, composed before
in a nobler verse-form,
praise about a destroyer of necklaces [generous man],
any man under the skirts of heaven?
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: Fornyrðislag (old-story metre):
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text:
It is composed about the ruler
who reddens the lips
of wolf and she-wolf
and colours weapons.
That will live for ever,
unless mankind perish,
the praise of princes,
or the worlds give way.
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: Bálkarlag (Bálkr's metre):
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text:
I raise bright
praise of the great king.
Before men is borne up
the earl's encomium.
What man might hear
praise of those sluggish in giving
composed in such a way,
[sluggish] with gold and treasures?
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: This is the distinction between these verse-forms: that in fornyrðislag there is in the first and third vísuorð (line) one stuðill (prop), and in the second and fourth line the höfuðstafr (chief stave) stands in the middle of the line, while in stikkalag there are two stuðlar (props), and the chief stave in the middle of the line. But in bálkarlag the props and the chief stave stand as in dróttkvætt (court metre).
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: Starkaðarlag (Starkaðr's metre):
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text:
I know as more worthy
those who give gold,
wield swords
and fit out warships,
of higher praise
than a stay-at-home,
the young princes,
and than a hoarder of wealth.
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text:
These princes are
the wisest of all,
the highest in rings,
the boldest of heart,
the worst to gold [most liberal],
the most daring in battle,
the most loyal to their retinue,
the nearest to good fortune.
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: Ljóðaháttr (song-metre):
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text:
A clear account
I have made of poetry;
thus a hundred of ten tens is reckoned.
Unworthy of praise
shall a man not be called,
if he can compose all verse-forms thus.
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text: Galdralag (incantation-metre):
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text:
I sought advancement,
I sought a meeting with the king,
I sought the glorious earl,
when I cut,
when I made [my ship] run,
the cold current with the keel,
the cold sea with the keel.
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10

records.text:
May they enjoy long life
and halls of wealth,
king and earl;
that is the poem's end.
May sooner fall
the earth into the sea,
propped with stone,
than the ruler's praise.
records.author: ai:claude-2026-10
